In doing so, he presents ideas that assume a basic difference between East and West in the way they responded to ancient civilization. By “the East,” he means the Arabs in particular.

For Becker, the key difference lies in what he calls humanism: a sense of the self, or the presence of a distinctly human and subjective emotional life within a people’s cultural and civilizational production.
This becomes the decisive basis of the distinction he draws between East and West.
The East, in his view, has a rational and logical tendency but does not possess “humanism.”

The West, by contrast, had already produced the idea of humanism through Christian thought, and this humanism was bound to reappear later. In Becker’s view, it is deeply rooted in the West. It appeared in the Roman period, returned during the Renaissance, and still appears today in different forms in different European countries.
According to Becker, this “decisive difference” between East and West explains why they responded differently to the heritage of Greek civilization:

“Differences of type and race, differences in geographical environment, and the independent historical development of each side mean that the heritage of the ancients”—by which he means the Greeks and Romans—“produced in the West a form of development completely different from the one it produced in the East.”
But what was it about the heritage of the ancients that supposedly produced such different reactions?
Becker answers through Werner Jaeger, who describes humanism as:
“the idea of civilization based on the ideal of the pure cultivation and education of the human being, an ideal created by the Greeks when they reached the highest stage of their development.”
For Becker, then, humanism in this sense is the central feature of Greek civilization.
Since he believes the East lacks this humanism while the West possesses it naturally, he concludes that the two regions had to respond differently to Greek civilization.
Becker says much more along these lines.

He denies that the Arabs created a civilization of their own or added anything fundamentally new to the civilizations of the countries they conquered. He argues that practically everything remained as it had been before, except that official and administrative documents that had once been written in Greek, Persian, or Coptic were now written in Arabic, while “nothing essential in the administration itself was changed.”
In other words, Becker sees no real human creative process in the relationship between the Arabs and the civilization of the ancients.
From this point of view, the East was interested in Greek writings only when they suited what he calls its “rational and logical tendency.”
But the “Greek spirit”—by which he means humanism—remained closed to the East. This included Greek lyric poetry, imaginative literature, and everything he regarded as most purely Greek.
So, in Becker’s formulation, the Greek heritage met ideas in the East, but in the West it met human beings.
To reinforce this argument, Becker turns to Goethe’s famous statement:
“East and West can no longer be separated.”
Becker interprets this to mean that the general view of the world and of life found in East and West is fundamentally very similar because both came from the same source.
By that source he means the Greek heritage.

So even the similarity between East and West, in Becker’s view, does not come from the historically and scientifically sound fact that human societies in different ages can share common forms of thought.
Instead, the similarity comes from the claim that both Eastern and Western views of life descend from the same Greek origin.
But even this similarity is only superficial for Becker, because he still believes that East and West responded to the Greek heritage in fundamentally different ways.
The idea that one part of humanity has a special claim to rational thought or humanism while another part does not is itself an ahistorical assumption.
And because this assumption rests on an unscientific theory of race, it is false at its foundation.
Becker refers more than once in his lecture to the factor of “race.”
But both rational thought and humanism are forms of consciousness shared by humanity as a whole.

Every human society is capable, simply because it is human, of developing both forms within its social consciousness and national culture. At a particular historical moment, one may become more dominant than the other.
But what determines this balance is not race or geography.
The decisive factor is the historical situation of each society: the form of its social relationships and the psychological outlook produced by its culture as a whole.
And historical conditions are never fixed. They are always moving and changing. As they change, they inevitably change the many relationships and factors that depend on them.
Becker’s judgments, however, appear to apply equally to East and West under all conditions and in every historical period.
It is true that Becker sometimes mentions “historical factors” alongside racial ones.
But what does he mean by “historical” in the first place?
When we look at his argument as a whole, these supposed historical factors appear frozen, static, and permanent.
In that sense, they are not historical at all.
Before Becker, the French philosopher Ernest Renan (1823–1892) had already made “race theory” the direct basis of his well-known judgments about “Arab philosophy.”
Renan carried conclusions from his comparative study of the Semitic languages into his study of philosophy.
As a scholar of Semitic languages, he followed a classification common among European linguists of his time, who divided peoples into “Semitic” and “Aryan” groups.
They based this distinction on similarities they believed they had found between Sanskrit and European languages.
Peoples whose languages they traced back to Sanskrit, including groups such as the Brahmins of India, were placed within the “Aryan” family together with European peoples.
Other peoples whose languages came from different linguistic roots, including the Arabs, were placed in another human family that they called the “Semitic race.”
Renan then added something further to this linguistic classification.
He turned it into a theory of hierarchy between the two supposed racial families in terms of cultural level and intellectual ability.
He placed the “Aryan race” above the “Semitic race.”
Renan says this quite openly. He even claims that he was the first to establish that the Semitic race was inferior to the Aryan race.
This theory of hierarchy between human “races” later became part of the theoretical foundation of Hitler’s Nazi ideology, an ideology hostile both to science and to humanity.
Renan’s judgments about Arab philosophy became widely known.
He may have been the first person in nineteenth-century Europe to popularize the claim that it was wrong to call the Greek philosophy transmitted into Arabic “Arab philosophy.”

According to him, what was called Arab philosophy was really no more than a body of writings produced as a reaction against Arabism in the regions of the Islamic Empire furthest from the Arabian Peninsula—places such as Samarkand, Bukhara, Córdoba, and Marrakesh.
These philosophical works were written in Arabic only because Arabic had become the language of science and religion throughout the Islamic world. In Renan’s view, that was the whole story.
Renan even rejects the claim that the Arabs preferred Aristotle to other Greek philosophers.
He argues that there was no genuine preference, because preference requires choice, and the Arabs had made no deliberate choice after reflection.
“The Arabs simply adopted Greek culture in the form in which it reached them…”
In the note that introduced the second edition of his book Averroes and Averroism, Renan repeated the same position:
“The Arabs did nothing more than adopt the whole Greek encyclopedia as the world encountered it around the seventh and eighth centuries.”
What concerns us here is not the judgment itself about Arab philosophy.
What matters at this point is the basis on which that judgment rests.
Renan makes that basis clear in the introduction to the first edition of his book, where he says openly:

“It is not from the Semitic race that we should expect lessons in philosophy. One of the strange ironies of history is that this race, which was able to give its religious creations such extraordinary power, produced almost nothing original in philosophy. Among the Semites, philosophy was little more than something borrowed from outside, without great fertility of its own—essentially an imitation of Greek philosophy…”
The danger of this racial “theory” lies in the fact that it became a wider intellectual current.
Renan was only one of its most prominent theorists.
After him, racial ideas became one of the foundations used in a number of Orientalist studies and formed part of imperialist ideology.
Among the Orientalists who continued this line of thought was Léon Gauthier, formerly a professor of history at the University of Algiers and a “well-known enthusiast for colonial rule.”
Gauthier added new claims to Renan’s distinction between Semites and Aryans.
He argued that the “Semitic mind” could see things only as separate and unconnected, while the “Aryan mind” was able to bring things together, connect them, and form them into a coherent whole.
Starting from this arbitrary racial distinction, he presents Islam as a strongly Semitic religion standing in opposition to Greek philosophy, which he presents as strongly Aryan.
He then places the Islamic philosophers between these two supposedly opposing worlds.
According to him, they tried with great skill to bridge the gap, but even the tools they used came from Greek philosophy itself.

Their work, on this account, was simply “Aryan” thinking trying to create a gradual connection between two opposing forms of thought: Islamic thought, supposedly based on separation, and Greek thought, supposedly based on connection.
Gauthier uses the same colonial racial framework when judging the Moroccan people.
Among the white peoples of the Mediterranean basin, he describes Moroccans as the culturally different group that had “remained far behind.”
Other Western Orientalists followed the same general current.
One was the German Orientalist Christian Lassen (1876), known for dividing peoples into Semitic and Aryan groups and for his hostility toward the “Semitic race.”
Another was Émile Bréhier, professor of the history of philosophy at the Sorbonne, who also supported the distinction between Semites and Aryans.
Starting from this idea, Bréhier speaks about the philosophers of Islam in much the same way as Renan.

He argues that although they wrote their philosophical works in Arabic, most were not Semitic in origin but Aryan. This, according to him, explains why they looked for their philosophical subjects in Greek thought and also in the Mazdakite ideas of Persia, which in turn were mixed with Indian ideas.
The Orientalist Stanla, known for his lectures at the Egyptian University on the history of philosophy, followed a similar approach.
He too begins with racial assumptions when explaining the history of philosophy and of Islam.
In discussing the meaning of Islam, for example, he says:

“…This absolute submission in everything, which is often an original characteristic of the Semites, is the defining principle of Islam and distinguishes it among peoples. Perhaps a vague awareness of a similar connection between this opposition and the religious instinct characteristic of the Arab people was what led Muḥammad to proclaim that he was the revealer of the true and original religion of Abraham and the Seal of the Prophets…”
Modern science has made the falsehood of dividing humanity according to “race” and racial characteristics so clear that there is no need for us to discuss the question at length here.
Specialized scientific works provide detailed evidence against it.
A readily accessible Arabic source on the subject is the recently published book The Racial Problem in Islam.
It summarizes the findings of modern anthropologists, sociologists, and psychologists—even bourgeois scholars—who have rejected the foundations of racial theories.
But we need to be careful here.
The fact that bourgeois scholars have been forced by modern scientific evidence to abandon racial theories does not mean that they have abandoned the social uses those theories served.
